problem: LLM-driven multi-robot planners either assume oracle access to global scene state in simulation or rely only on robot-to-robot sharing, so partial observability forces heavy exploration or larger teams. Prior work does not model how ambient indoor IoT sensing can be fused into a shared semantic state for planning.
motivation: Many indoor spaces already have low-cost IoT sensors such as CCTV that give persistent, building-wide context beyond onboard perception. Using them could cut redundant exploration, path length and LLM planning cost. This needs a benchmark that strictly enforces partial observability so no agent is omniscient.
key_idea: Fuse robot observations and VLM-processed IoT/CCTV event logs into a global semantic state on a coordination hub, and let an LLM online planner produce parallel DAG plans over it (Robot-to-Everything, R2X).
insight: The ablation IR -> R2R -> R2X shows robot-to-robot sharing drives task feasibility (SR 66% -> 92%), while IoT information mainly reduces exploration (path 99 m -> 88 m, tokens 47,875 -> 42,438). Robustness tests show omission of CCTV detections is harmless to success (92% even at 100% missing, only longer paths), whereas corrupted semantic status reports linearly reduce success because they make the planner skip preconditions. Planner capability matters a lot (Llama-3.1-8b 6% vs GPT-4.1 92%).
method: Benchmark: 85 multi-room AI2-THOR environments (10 ArchitecTHOR homes for navigation+manipulation, 75 RoboTHOR apartments for navigation-only); each robot knows only its current view and visited areas.
IoT simulation: static CCTV cameras cover ~50% of house area randomly; a VLM (Qwen-VL) turns the feeds into time-stamped text event logs streamed to the hub.

Global semantic state: the hub keeps W_t = (robot, object, area states); objects carry type, position, parent receptacle, binary dynamic properties, room, source (robot/IoT ID) and timestamp; a fusion function F updates it from all sources.

LLM online planner: the LLM gets the task, world state, robot skills and an output schema, and returns a dependency-graph (DAG) plan with action nodes (action, params, required skills, preferred robot).

Parallel orchestrator and monitor: idle robots are matched to ready nodes by proximity, inventory and camera horizon; an async monitor handles ActionDone, stalls and IoTUpdate events, halting only affected robots and triggering replanning.
Action execution: state-aware low-level subroutines (e.g. slice_object handles inventory, navigation and retries) behind a fault-tolerant interface.

setting.backbone: GPT-4.1 (frozen) as main planner; Gemma-3-27b-it and Llama-3.1-8b-instruct as ablations; Qwen-VL for CCTV to text
setting.observation: egocentric robot view plus visited-area memory, plus text event logs from simulated CCTV/IoT
setting.action_space: high-level semantic actions (navigate, pickup, put, toggle, slice, etc.) in a DAG, executed by low-level executors
setting.simulator: AI2-THOR (ArchitecTHOR, RoboTHOR); plus real-world test with Stretch robots
setting.privileged: none for robots; IoT/CCTV observations are the intended X channel (simulated object detections/device states)

numbers_note: Results are on the paper's own IndoorR2X benchmark (SR, action steps, path length, LLM tokens), which is not in the canonical list, so no entries are given. Main R2X (GPT-4.1, 3 robots): SR 92%, 108 steps, 88 m, 42,438 tokens. R2R: 92%, 116, 99 m, 47,875. IR: 66%, 186, 137 m, 54,572. Adapted SMART-LLM: 88%, 124, 119 m, 43,397. Adapted EMOS: 88%, 135, 122 m, 51,394. Gemma-3-27b: 64%, 113, 94 m, 26,753. Llama-3.1-8b: 6%, 47, 55 m, 50,512. Team-size and failure results are only in figures.
results: On the IndoorR2X benchmark with GPT-4.1 and three robots, R2X reaches 92% SR with the fewest steps (108), shortest path (88 m) and fewest tokens (42,438). It beats adapted SMART-LLM and EMOS (88% SR, 119-122 m) and reduces path length by over 26% versus SMART-LLM. SR stays above 90% up to five robots, degrades mildly with IoT latency (87% at delay 10), and is robust to missing detections but sensitive to corrupted status.
limitations: Centralized hub and planner: coordination overhead grows with team size and needs hierarchical or decentralized methods for larger fleets.
IoT observations are simulated (CCTV coverage ~50%, VLM logs); only omission and status corruption were tested, and stale or wrong VLM outputs can cause unrecoverable errors.
Real-world validation is only qualitative on a small three-room demo with no quantitative results; baselines are adapted rather than original.
